en: The Sūtra on the Ritual Manual for the Samādhi of the Installation of Images of All Tathāgatas,
translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao San Da Fu, Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial.
Translated by the Dharma-transmitting Master, the Subject Shi Hu, by Imperial Decree.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered a samādhi called the Vajra Image-Installation Samādhi of All Tathāgatas.
Emerging from samādhi,
he spoke of those clay sculptures, paintings, and carvings that adorn all Buddhas as well as the assemblies of sages and holy ones.
Regarding the ritual procedures for consecrating an image and performing celebratory praises:
one who wishes to create a Buddha image must first identify an Ācārya who is thoroughly proficient in the ten types of rules.
Furthermore, one must thoroughly understand all the marks of the Buddha’s body in their complete perfection,
as well as the proportions and measurements of its various parts,
for the purposes of rites such as pacification and enrichment.
He was fully proficient in all matters concerning the rituals of mantras, mudrās, and dhāraṇīs.
Nevertheless, he constructed various images of the honored ones within the temples, halls, and stupas of that monastery.
However, there were instances where the iconographic features of the Buddha images he produced were incomplete.
One must not install images for celebratory praise;
if the ritual forms and characteristics are incomplete,
it will cause those sentient beings to experience great suffering and fear in both the present life and the future.
Therefore, with a single-minded resolve, one should seek to achieve perfection.
Once perfection has been attained,
one should [entrust it] to the previously designated Dharma-ācārya.
By following the ritual procedures of the mantras,
one invites the Buddhas, installs the images, makes offerings, and performs celebratory praises;
thus, one immediately attains the presence of the Tathāgatas and the holy ones.
The merit of the descent [of the deity] and the joy of sympathetic rejoicing is accomplished.
If, after the image has been completed for a long time,
one does not perform the consecration and celebratory rites for the installation of the image, [the merit is lost].
In time thereafter, one will instead encounter misfortune;
even if others were to make offerings or pay homage,
there would ultimately be no benefit or merit.
Just as an ignorant person who lacks the proper physical characteristics causes the world to treat them with contempt,
so too does it happen if an ācārya requests the installation of a Buddha image [without the requisite qualifications].
If one does not understand the Dharma and lacks the proper ritual procedures,
it is like putting ghee into ashes;
if one performs a homa under such conditions, there will certainly be no fruit or reward.
Therefore, one must ensure that the crafted image possesses the complete and perfect marks,
and that the ritual procedures for the consecration and celebration of the image are fully observed,
so that all sentient beings may obtain great merit and rewards.
At that time, a certain bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, the Buddha-body is without marks;
it is like empty space, pervading all places."
"How is it that you now speak of establishing images of the Buddha?
The Buddha said, "Listen attentively now;
I have practiced for a long time."
It is taught that this Dharmakāya is signless and unconditioned;
it pervades all places like empty space,
being inherently quiescent from the beginning, neither arising nor ceasing.
How should one install an image? Now,
for the sake of sentient beings who have newly resolved their minds [for enlightenment],
so that they may obtain merit, I shall explain the method for installing an image, performing celebratory praise, and performing the rite of purification.
When intending to construct a maṇḍala,
first select an auspicious star and an auspicious day;
then, at a pure location within a consecrated boundary, establish the site.
Arrange parasols, banners, streamers, incense, flowers, lamps,
and fruit offerings. Then, have the ācārya, according to the ritual procedures,
single-mindedly invoke [the deities] first within the boundaries of the consecrated site, both above and below.
Using five-colored powders and marking lines, construct a maṇḍala.
Invite the Tathāgatas of the five families along with their retinues of bodhisattvas and others;
this must be performed according to this fundamental ritual manual.
One must not invoke [the deities] according to other rituals.
Furthermore, when the ācārya enters the Buddha hall or temple to install an image,
he must use his wrists and fingers.
Adorned with bracelets, armlets, rings, and other ornaments,
the ācārya and his disciples should single-mindedly visualize the Tathāgata’s all-perfect marks.
Thereafter, joining the palms in reverent salutation, one gazes upon the noble sages.
According to the ritual procedures, one offers *argha*, incense, lamps, and fruit using pure incense, flowers, scented water, and lamps.
Having made the offering, enter meditative absorption with a mind free from doubt and recite this mantra three times:
*samaya-stadvaṃ samaya-stadvaṃ*. Having recited this mantra, make this supplication:
Just as all Buddhas abide in the Tuṣita Heaven,
and just as the Buddha dwelt within the womb of Queen Māyā,
may the Buddha, out of his compassion, likewise abide here.
"I pray that the Buddha will remain forever for the sake of his disciple [Name],
who has resolved to attain bodhicitta and offers this incense and flowers as an offering.
Having thus invited the image of the Buddha:
Furthermore, when conferring the precepts upon the donor's disciples,
all matters concerning the rules for offerings and ritual procedures must strictly follow the instructions of the ācārya; one must not be negligent.
Causing that donor to obtain great karmic fruit,
they invite the Tathāgata to dwell upon his seat,
offering incense, flowers, lamps, fruits, food, and drink.
Recite the mantra and present the offering of argha water.
All the Buddha images should be arranged facing east and covered with yellow cloth.
The Ācārya performs the visualization,
imagining the Buddha as a single mass of fire;
he recites this mantra seven times and hurls white mustard seeds [into the fire].
Oṃ sarvabāpasphoṭanahana vajrāya svāhā. Having recited this mantra, [one should proceed].
Furthermore, visualize the Tathāgata as having a body of true reality, with all marks fully perfected.
Then, place the three syllables Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ upon three locations on the body of the image, placing the syllable Oṃ on the crown of the head.
Place the syllable *A* upon the mouth and the syllable *HŪṂ* upon the heart.
If one is able to recite the root mantra of the tutelary deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), it need only be placed upon the heart.
If one performs the mudrā of invocation, the vajra-mudrā, or the hook-mudrā according to the ritual rules, or if a person lacks the capacity,
one should have them performed according to one's ability.
The vessels used may be made of gold, silver, precious gems, copper, stone, earthenware, wood, conch shells, or tree leaves.
All may perform the offering of argha.
If one uses a copper vessel for the argha within the ritual,
it is most excellent, like gold or stone.
The Buddha image was old and dark;
one should apply fragrant oil upon it and wash it clean using a brush made of grass.
Then, using songs, praises, and music, have the young girls dance and sing, while further reciting the incense-oil mantra:
*Oṃ sarvatathāgatagāyavīśodhani svāhā*. If using auspicious vases, employ five or eight.
Anoint it with white sandalwood incense;
fill that flask with various types of fragrant water and immediately perform empowerment upon it.
Furthermore, have a young girl join the threads together.
Dye it with five colors to make it a fine, fresh wrapping for the circumference of the vase.
Furthermore, place the five precious gems, the five medicines, flowers, fruits, and so forth into the auspicious vase (*bhadraghaṭa*).
Recite either the *Uṣṇīṣavijaya* mantra or the *Sitatapatrā* mantra.
One may perform empowerment by scattering white mustard seeds,
or it is also permissible to recite the mantra for pacifying calamities.
This is likewise done when bathing a Buddha image.
First, apply fragrant oil, then use the powdered leaves of the nyagrodha tree and the udumbara tree.
Place five kinds of grains and five types of pure water in a copper vessel.
Bathe the Buddha image,
and then cause all the disciples and the multitude to recite verses of praise and various songs and music.
Regarding these as auspicious sounds,
one should joyfully honor the sacred image according to the ritual of consecration (*abhiṣeka*);
then, one recites the mantra of the Bodhisattva Locanā, which is capable of removing all defilements.
Having recited this mantra— Oṃ sarvarājopahāraṇa svāhā—
the Ācārya says:
Just as the Buddha’s body was bathed at the time of his descent into birth,
so too is it for all Tathāgatas.
I now bathe the image of the Buddha with pure, supreme water.
Furthermore, recite the Consecration Mantra:
Oṃ sarvatathāgatābhiṣekasamayaśrīye hūṃ. This is for the merit of a painted image.
Reflecting upon the merits depicted therein by means of a mirror,
one should write the five aforementioned kinds of pure water upon the mirror and bathe the reflection within it.

If one has previously [prepared] images made of gold, silver, and so forth, as well as painted scroll-images (paṭa), once the ritual bathing is completed, one should immediately recite the mantra for donning the robes:
Oṃ vajravāsasi svāhā. Next, recite the mantra for placing the ear-ornaments.
Oṃ karaṇa-mārudharaṇa hūṃ. Next, recite the mantra for installing the hair-tuft:
Oṃ sarvakīrṣāvadhāraṇa svāhā. Next, recite the mantra for installing the fingernails.
Oṃ sarvaśuṇḍakhañjanāraja svāhā. Next, recite the mantra for establishing the beard and mustache:
Oṃ sarvasamasurudhāraṇa hūṃ hūṃ hiṃ liṃ. Next, recite the mantra for offering the scented unguent.
Oṃ vajragandhe svāhā. Next, recite the mantra for adorning:
Oṃ vajrapraṇavatuṣṇī svāhā. Having recited this mantra, [proceed].
Having entered the maṇḍala according to the ritual for empowerment, one recites the samaya-mantra of the deity together with the image of the Buddha.
Oṃ hūṃ traḷokriḥ. Having recited this mantra, [one should proceed].
Thus, having placed the Buddha image facing east while wearing a crown,
one causes that patron to obtain great benefit and merit.
Next, one should perform offerings with incense, flowers, and so forth.
First, recite the mantra for offering flowers:
Oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ. Having recited this mantra, speak these words:
"This flower is most excellent; it grows either in water or on land."
"I now offer this with a sincere heart; may the Buddha graciously accept it.
Next, recite the incense offering mantra:
*Oṃ vajra dhūpe*. Having recited this mantra, speak as follows:
This incense is most excellent, whether it be natural incense or blended incense.
With a sincere heart, I now offer it; may the Buddha graciously accept it.
Next, recite the mantra for scented ointment.
Oṃ vajragandhe svāhā. Having recited this mantra, he says:
"This is supreme and most excellent incense; may the Buddha please accept it."
Next, recite the lamp mantra:
Oṃ vajra-dīpe svāhā. Having recited this mantra, say:
"This is the lamp offering—whether a ghee lamp or an oil lamp—whose light dispels darkness."
I now offer this with a sincere heart; may the Buddha graciously accept it.
May all ignorance and darkness be dispelled.
Next, recite the food mantra.
Oṃ pinupadapratigṛhṇa hūṃ svāhā. Having recited this mantra, he spoke as follows.
This is the supreme food offering, possessing all colors, fragrances, and exquisite flavors.
I now offer this with a sincere heart; may the Buddha graciously accept it.
Thus, the ritual procedures for the offering have been fully completed.
Furthermore, for the purpose of opening the eyes of a Buddha image,
one should perform it as if applying collyrium to the eyes;
then, recite the *Kāyalocanā-mantra* twice.
Oṃ cakru cakru samanta cakru viśodhani svāhā. Oṃ nītra paṭalu pahāraṇa hili. Next, recite the mantra for the Buddha’s entry into meditative absorption.
Oṃ nīle nīlasamādhiṣṭhita prīṇaya svāhā. Having recited this mantra:
Furthermore, he causes the donor’s disciple to enter the maṇḍala.
The ācārya says:
"You have now requested me to install the Buddha image for your peace and prosperity."
I have now completed all the ritual procedures for you;
you should receive initiation and recite this mantra:
*samaya-sattvaṃ*. Next, perform the homa.
One may perform [the recitation] one thousand, five hundred, or two hundred and fifty times.
If constructing a homa hearth, it should be made square;
use [fuel from] a tree that yields white milky sap.
Place wet firewood into the hearth,
and further perform homa using a mixture of ghee, curd, honey, and the five grains;
this will bring about the pacification of calamities and the increase of prosperity for oneself and all disciples.
Then recite the homa mantra:
Oṃ vajrayuṣe svāhā. This is the homa mantra. Next, recite the longevity-increasing mantra.
AGACCA HARIPIṄGALA NEPATA JIHVA RŪHIṬA KṢAṆE HIṆA NANA PARYEṆA TSAME KĀRYAṂ KURU SVĀHĀ. This is the mantra for increasing longevity.
Next, recite the mantra for pacifying and increasing:
Oṃ vajrapuṣṭaye svāhā. This is the mantra for pacifying and increasing.
Next, for the deity Agni, arrange a seat within the homa fire-pit and perform the visualization.
Visualize that within the three sections of the homa fire-pit:
Leave one portion empty for the seat of the Fire Deity (Agni).
Oṃ supratīṣṭhita vajra svāhā. This is the mantra for installing the Fire Deity.
Next, offer incense, flowers, and so forth to the World-Protectors (Lokapālas) and Īśāna.
Then recite the mantra of the World-Protectors:
*Indrāya svāhā*. Having recited this mantra, [proceed].
Having performed music, song, dance, and so forth as a send-off, he addressed them, saying:
"The extensive Buddhist services and offerings performed above were for the most part not in accordance with the Dharma.
O Brahma devas, sons of gods, and all you hosts of deities who have come here..."
For the sake of their patrons, following this ritual procedure,
perform great pacification and enrichment in all places; then,
proceed to that buddha-field and again issue an invitation for them to descend.
The deities of earth, water, fire, wind, and so forth shall go to their respective realms and,
with minds of goodness, affection, and reverence,
protect the installed Buddha images for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
May the patrons, their descendants, and their retinues,
as well as the ācārya and all his disciples, universally obtain auspiciousness.
This applies when performing the mandala ritual at an auspicious time.
The first, second, third, fourth, fifth, eleventh, and twelfth months; or,
regarding the days used within the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa),
the second, third, seventh, tenth, thirteenth, and fifteenth days.
It may also be performed during the dark fortnight;
furthermore, one must proceed on an auspicious day under a favorable lunar mansion (nakṣatra) and planetary alignment (tithi) before the rite may be enacted.
If the asterisms Āśleṣā, Pūrvabhādrapadā, Uttarābhādrapadā, Svātī, Jyeṣṭhā, Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, Abhijit, Puṣya,
and Pūrvaphalgunī are present, these are the most auspicious stars;
in seeking any undertaking, all shall be accomplished.
If the constellation Jīva attains the fulfillment of the ritual practice, one's requests will surely be granted,
and one will additionally gain external kinsmen.
This also applies to the constellations Mūla, Puṣya, and Svāti.
One will gain the respect and affection of others as well as material wealth.
If it falls under the lunar mansion of Shen (參), one will attain the pacification of calamities;
if under Ji (箕), one will obtain long-lived descendants.
If the constellation Śravaṇā prevails, one will constantly achieve auspicious matters;
if Ārdrā prevails, one will attain all that is most excellent;
and if Hasta or Viśākhā prevails, one will obtain happiness and fulfillment of one's desires.
If Jupiter, Mercury, and Venus are the most auspicious and virtuous,
and these three stars coincide with the day of the solar mansion,
then by performing the ritual procedures for consecrating images and offering praise, one shall obtain the highest merit.
If the third, seventh, sixth, tenth, and eleventh stars are among these five stars,
and they are in conjunction with the moon,
it is most auspicious for all undertakings.
If the second, sixth, tenth, and eleventh lunar mansions are in conjunction with Mercury,
it is likewise highly auspicious.
If the second, seventh, ninth, and eleventh lunar mansions are in conjunction with Jupiter, [it is likewise highly auspicious].
Using these together for invocation, consecration, and purification is most excellent and highly auspicious.
If the sixth, seventh, or tenth lunar mansions coincide with the planet Venus,
using them together is likewise highly auspicious.
If the first, third, or fifth lunar mansions can destroy one's wealth and possessions,
the ācārya should thus skillfully understand the power of the constellations.
For example, if on the day of performing the ritual one obtains favorable planetary alignments, [the rite will succeed].
Whatever task is undertaken shall certainly be accomplished within a single moment.
If one installs an image and performs celebratory praises, the merit obtained will be supreme;
one shall undoubtedly attain the rank of a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) or the position of a great king.
Furthermore, if the celestial bodies are in harmonious alignment and there are no obstacles or difficulties whatsoever,
the Buddha images and stūpas established therein will achieve fulfillment in every lifetime and birth, and people will obtain blessings and merit.
If there are image-makers and various artisans involved, one should provide them with wealth and silk,
and comfort them with kind words so that they do not suffer privation;
only then will it accord with the ritual requirements.
Any food remaining from the offerings made to the Tathāgata,
if consumed by a person, will cause all their transgressions to be extinguished. The Ācārya then instructs the patron,
establishing a karmic connection to increase their merit and bestowing upon them all gold, silver, wealth, silks, elephants, horses, and carriages.
According to one's capacity, offer gifts with a sincere heart to bring joy to the ācārya;
the noble ones will likewise rejoice.
Furthermore, one should provide offerings of wealth and food to monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen according to one's ability, so that their merit may be perfected.
During the first watch of the night, one should perform great music, singing, dancing, and play banners, flowers, conchs, and cymbals.
Furthermore, the patron and their retinue, surrounding and paying homage,
must all offer the various articles of worship within the maṇḍala to the ācārya.
One must not break it for use elsewhere,
nor may one give it to another bhikṣu;
such actions would be inconsistent with the proper dharma.
When the ritual of the altar is completed,
one should immediately collect the altar implements;
if they consist of five-colored powders, they should be cast into a river.
Wash and wipe the ground of the altar with *kumāśaya* pure water.
Perform the ritual purification according to the dharma so that merit may be accomplished.
This is from the *Sarvatathāgata-pratimā-sthāpana-samādhi-vidhi-sūtra*.
